evidence.title: Eilis Flynn
evidence.text: Eilis Flynn (b. Elizabeth Myrtle Smith, on a May 12 in Tacoma, Washington, United States), is an American author of four fantasy romance novels for the publisher, Cerridwen Press.

evidence.title: Eilis Flynn
evidence.text: She also has written for DC Comics using the name Elizabeth M. Smith.

evidence.title: Jane Feather
evidence.text: Jane Feather, née "Jane Robotham" (born 1945 in Cairo, Egypt) is a popular British–American writer of historical romance novels.

evidence.title: Jane Feather
evidence.text: In 1984 she wrote five contemporary romances under the pseudonym Claudia Bishop.

evidence.title: Jane Feather
evidence.text: She now is a New York Times bestselling, award–winning writer and she has more than ten million romance novels in print.

evidence.title: Harper Allen
evidence.text: Harper Allen is a Canadian writer of contemporary and fantasy romance novels since 1998.

evidence.title: Sarah MacLean
evidence.text: Sarah MacLean (born December 17, 1978) is a New York Times bestselling American author of young adult novels and romance novels.

evidence.title: Sarah MacLean
evidence.text: Her first adult romance novel, "Nine Rules to Break When Romancing a Rake" debuted on the New York Times Bestseller List, where it stayed for four weeks.

evidence.title: Sarah MacLean
evidence.text: Since then, all of her adult romance novels have been on the New York Times and USA Today bestseller lists.

evidence.title: Sarah MacLean
evidence.text: Since February 2014, MacLean has written a monthly romance novel review column for The Washington Post.

evidence.title: Sarah MacLean
evidence.text: She is a two-time winner of the Romance Writers of America RITA Award for Best Historical Romance for "A Rogue by Any Other Name" in 2013 and "No Good Duke Goes Unpunished" in 2014.

evidence.title: Twilight (novel series)
evidence.text: Twilight is a series of four vampire-themed fantasy romance novels by American author Stephenie Meyer.

evidence.title: Twilight (novel series)
evidence.text: Released annually from 2005 through 2008, the four books chart the later teen years of Isabella "Bella" Swan, a girl who moves to Forks, Washington, and falls in love with a 104-year-old vampire named Edward Cullen.

evidence.title: Twilight (novel series)
evidence.text: The series is told primarily from Bella's point of view, with the epilogue of "Eclipse" and Part II of "Breaking Dawn" being told from the viewpoint of character Jacob Black, a werewolf.

evidence.title: Twilight (novel series)
evidence.text: The unpublished "Midnight Sun" is a retelling of the first book, "Twilight", from Edward Cullen's point of view.

evidence.title: Twilight (novel series)
evidence.text: The novella "The Short Second Life of Bree Tanner", which tells the story of a newborn vampire who appeared in "Eclipse", was published on June 5, 2010, as a hardcover book and on June 7 as a free online ebook. ""

evidence.title: House of Night
evidence.text: House of Night is a series of young adult vampire-themed fantasy novels by American author P. C. Cast and her daughter Kristin Cast.

evidence.title: House of Night
evidence.text: It follows the adventures of Zoey Redbird, a sixteen-year-old girl who has just become a "fledgling vampyre" and is required to attend the House of Night boarding school in Tulsa, Oklahoma.

evidence.title: House of Night
evidence.text: Books in the series have been on the "New York Times" Best Seller list for 63 weeks and have sold over seven million copies in North America, and more than ten million books worldwide, in 39 countries.

evidence.title: House of Night

evidence.title: The Dark Heroine
evidence.text: The Dark Heroine is a series of vampire-themed fantasy romance novels written by English author Abigail Gibbs, published by HarperCollins in 2012.

evidence.title: The Dark Heroine
evidence.text: The first novel in the series, "Dinner with a Vampire," revolves around London-born Violet Lee, who is kidnapped and held hostage by a Royal Family of vampires known as the Varns.

evidence.title: The Dark Heroine
evidence.text: The series is told from both Violet Lee and Kaspar Varn's perspective, the latter being heir to the Vamperic Throne in the novel.

evidence.title: Night Huntress
evidence.text: Night Huntress is a series of "New York Times" bestselling urban fantasy romance novels by author Jeaniene Frost.

evidence.title: Night Huntress
evidence.text: The first novel was published in 2007 by Avon and takes place in a world where supernatural creatures exist but are not known to the general public at large.

evidence.title: Night Huntress
evidence.text: The series initially focused around the character of half-vampire Catherine "Cat" Crawfield and her full-vampire lover Bones, but eventually shifted focus to other characters such as Vlad Tepesh, a character that Frost had initially not planned to include.

evidence.title: Tagalog pocketbooks
evidence.text: According to Tatin Yang in the article "Romansang Pinoy: A day with Tagalog romance novels", Tagalog romance paperbacks were thin Philippine versions of romance novel books that could be found at the bottom shelves of the romance section of bookstores, wrapped and bound with book covers that are decorated with Philippine comics-styled illustrations, such as "a barrio landscape with a badly dressed guy and girl locked in an embrace".

evidence.title: Tagalog pocketbooks
evidence.text: As a form of "escapist fiction" (escapism) and "commercial literature", Tagalog romance novels generally follow a "strict romance formula", meaning the narratives have happy endings (a factor influencing the salability of the novel), the protagonists are wealthy, good-looking, smart, and characters that cannot die.

evidence.title: Tagalog pocketbooks
evidence.text: Normally, the hero or heroine of the story falls in love and "goes crazy" over the admired person.

evidence.title: Tagalog pocketbooks
evidence.text: However, later authors of Tagalog romance novels deviated from portraying so-called "damsel-in-distress and knight-in-shining-armor characters".

evidence.title: Tagalog pocketbooks
evidence.text: Contemporary writers also turned away from writing "rags-to-riches plots".

evidence.title: Tagalog pocketbooks
evidence.text: The stereotypical norm had been replaced by the incorporation of storylines with "interesting scenes, characters [who are ready to face challenges or to sacrifice themselves for the benefit of other people], dialogues, and new angles to old plots".

evidence.title: Tagalog pocketbooks
evidence.text: Authors such as Maria Teresa Cruz San Diego, who used the pen names Maia Jose and Tisha Nicole, ventured into the fantasy romance genre, and into topics that are related to politics, ecology, gender issues, prostitution, mail-order bride syndicates, white slavery, non-governmental organizations, and breastfeeding programs.

evidence.title: Tagalog pocketbooks
evidence.text: Apart from writing about ideal lovers (men and women) and ideal situations, other novelists wrote about true-to-life settings, or at least based the stories from personal experiences.

evidence.title: Tagalog pocketbooks
evidence.text: Thus, Tagalog romance novels came to mirror or replicate the "roles that women and men play" in Philippine society.

evidence.title: Stephenie Meyer
